title: Building an offer that justifies a higher rate for Locksmith and door installation
audience: Locksmith and door installation operators who attend lockouts, rekey locks and fit replacement hardware for homes, rentals and small businesses.
learningOutcomes: Write an offer that states the attendance, the work and the after-hours terms as separate lines
Show what certainty and protection the price includes, and what it leaves out
Price the offer from value and cost, then compare it with published vendor ranges

instruction.heading: Sell the result and the attendance, both in writing
instruction.body: A lockout customer buys getting back in, and certainty about what it will cost. A headline such as 'attendance from $29' does not show the full price. A Victorian vendor listing warns that a lockout advertised at $29 or $45 usually quotes only the attendance, not the work (The Quote Yard, Victoria, published 26 September 2026). A clear offer states the attendance, the opening method, any rekey or make-safe work as separate lines, and any after-hours surcharge.

instruction.heading: Use the vendor ranges as a check, not as your price
instruction.body: The Quote Yard's Victorian estimates are vendor figures, not regulator data. They give a business-hours callout of $95 to $190, an after-hours callout of $190 to $460, a cylinder rekey of $48 to $130, and a supply-and-fit of a residential lock of $180 to $620. Set your price from your own cost, then check it against the ranges that match the work you do, and say which of your prices sit above or below them and why.

instruction.heading: Offer three levels that each add something visible
instruction.body: A good level might be attendance and opening. A better level adds a rekey of the cylinder. A best level adds a supply-and-fit of a new lock with a written key register. Show each level as its own written line, not as a hidden extra added after attendance. The customer can then choose the level that suits the situation.

instruction.heading: Written terms, and approval before extra work
instruction.body: A written quote becomes binding once it is accepted, so the scope and exclusions must be clear. Western Australian guidance says a tradesperson must get permission before extra work and cannot do extra work first and ask for payment later. Put the after-hours surcharge, the parts and the rekey in the quote, so a property manager can approve each line before attendance. New South Wales requires variations to a residential building contract to be in writing and signed by both parties.

instruction.heading: Guarantees you can keep
instruction.body: Consumer guarantees for services apply and cannot be removed by contract. A return visit within a stated period for a lock you fitted is a guarantee you control. Set the period from your own records, and do not promise to repair other people's doors or frames.

procedure: Write the outcome in one sentence a customer would repeat, such as 'you are back inside tonight, and the lock is secure'.
Write the attendance, the opening method, the rekey and any after-hours surcharge as separate lines.
List what the customer must provide, such as access and proof they can authorise the work, and what is excluded, such as the replacement of a damaged door.
Add one certainty element, such as a photo of the lock before and after, and a key register for any rekey.
Set the return-visit period you can keep, then price from cost and check the result against the vendor ranges for the same work.
State one all-in total for each level, say whether GST is included, and record the offer.

workedExamples.situation: A property manager's tenant is locked out at 9 pm on a Saturday. The manager also asks for the cylinder to be rekeyed in case the tenant's key is lost. The scenario is illustrative.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How should the quote be written, and what can the locksmith say about the price?
workedExamples.reasoning: The quote shows the after-hours attendance and the rekey as separate lines, so the property manager can approve each one before the locksmith attends. The vendor's Victorian estimates are an after-hours lockout all up at $260 to $620, a rekey at $48 to $130, and an after-hours callout alone at $190 to $460 (The Quote Yard, Victoria, vendor estimates, 26 September 2026). A combined quote would fall near the sum of the two lines. The locksmith sets his own after-hours surcharge from his own cost, rather than from those ranges. He does not state a Victorian licence status in the quote, because the research did not settle it. He checks it with the regulator first.

equipmentAndPpe: Quote template with the attendance, rekey and after-hours lines shown separately
Key register template for rekeys and new lock supply
Photo record of the lock before and after work
PPE as set by the site's own rules and {{business:safety.required_ppe}}

commonErrors.error: Advertising the attendance fee and leaving the work price out
commonErrors.prevention: Show the attendance, the work and any after-hours surcharge as separate written lines.

commonErrors.error: Adding an after-hours surcharge after the job is done
commonErrors.prevention: State the surcharge before attendance and get the customer's approval.

commonErrors.error: Promising a return visit with no stated period
commonErrors.prevention: Set a period you can keep and write it into the offer.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business guidance only. The ACCC says misleading statements about prices are prohibited. Show one total with GST status. This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority.

Victoria: the licence position for locksmiths is unresolved in the research and must be checked before you quote Victorian work. A Legislative Council petition presented in February 2026 asks for a definition of 'locksmith' in the Private Security Act 2004, which suggests the term is not defined there now. An industry body says the amended Act lists security equipment installation as a security activity, but it does not say whether a locksmith falls within that term. Do not state a Victorian licence requirement until the regulator confirms it.

New South Wales: locksmiths must be licensed. The licensing body is the Security Licensing and Enforcement Directorate (SLED) of the NSW Police Force. The guidance lists penalties of up to $55,000 and/or two years' imprisonment for individuals, or $110,000 for corporations.

Queensland: locksmiths must hold a security equipment installer licence under the Security Providers Act 1993. South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, the ACT and the Northern Territory were not checked in the research, so check the rule in each of those states before you work there.

qualityStandard: Every offer shows the attendance, the work and any after-hours surcharge as separate lines.
Every quote shows one total with GST status and a validity date.
Every extra task is approved in writing before it is done, and any state licence check is recorded before work starts.
documentationEvidence: Written offer with the attendance, work and after-hours lines
Key register for any rekey or new lock supplied
Record of the state licence check made before work started
summary: Show the attendance and the work as separate lines, not one advertised fee.
Use vendor ranges as a check against your own cost.
Check the state licence rule before you quote, because Victoria's position is unresolved.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which part of a locksmith's offer does the customer buy?
options: The outcome, with a clear price and certainty
Your hourly rate on its own
How long you have worked in the trade

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a guarantee in your offer be?
options: Something you can deliver and afford, such as a return visit for a stated period
Impossible to claim on in any case
Available only to repeat customers you know personally

knowledgeChecks.question: A vendor advertises a lockout at $29. What does this lesson say the price usually covers?
options: The whole job, including any rekey or replacement lock
The attendance only, not the work
Parts and labour but not travel
